pages.lead: The cheapest storage is rarely the one with the lowest headline price. It is the one that is the right size, on the right terms, holding only things worth keeping. Here is how to get there.

sections.html:
The most common way to overpay for storage is not a bad price. It is a unit that is too big. Empty floor space costs exactly the same as full floor space.

Most people size up out of caution, then pay for that caution every month. Make a list of the large items, estimate the boxes, and pack upwards: stacked boxes use height you are already paying for.

Our unit size guide turns square feet into rooms and boxes, and how to pack a storage unit shows how to fit more into less.

  • Insurance, and whether it is compulsory.
  • Padlocks, admin fees and set-up charges.

sections.h2: 5. Do not pay to store a decision
sections.html:
Storage is brilliant for things you will use again. It is an expensive way to postpone deciding about things you will not. A sideboard nobody wants costs nothing in the loft and something every month in a unit.

Spend one afternoon sorting before you move anything. Sell, donate or recycle what you would not pay to keep. Our decluttering guide has a simple method.

sections.h2: Start with a list, not a guess
sections.html:
The most common sizing mistake is to guess from the number of rooms in your house. Two people moving out of identical three-bedroom homes can need very different space: one has a loft full of boxes and a piano, the other has already sold half the furniture.

So start with a list. Walk round with a notepad or your phone and write down every large item: beds, sofas, wardrobes, tables, white goods, bikes, garden furniture. Then estimate your boxes. A standard medium moving box is roughly 45 cm on each side, and a typical room of everyday things tends to fill somewhere between ten and twenty of them once you are honest about cupboards and under-bed storage.

Big, awkward items decide the floor area. Boxes decide how high you need to stack. Keep the two separate in your head and sizing gets much easier.

We quote floor area in square feet. One square foot is about 0.093 square metres, so to convert, multiply by 0.093. To go the other way, one square metre is about 10.76 square feet.

pages.title: How to Pack a Storage Unit | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: How to pack a storage unit so everything fits and stays findable: boxes, labels, loading order and aisles. A practical guide from Blackpool.
h1: How to pack a storage unit
so you can find things later
pages.lead: A well-packed unit holds more, protects better and saves you an afternoon of digging when you need one thing from the back. Here is a method that works for homes and businesses alike.

sections.h2: Before you pack a single box
sections.html:
Packing for storage is different from packing for a move. On moving day, boxes are opened within a week. In storage, they might sit for months, and you may need to find one particular thing halfway through.

So spend half an hour planning first. Decide what will need to come out during the storage period (paperwork, seasonal clothes, tools) and what will not (spare furniture, the good china). The first group goes near the front. The second goes at the back and can be stacked high.

Then clean and dry everything. Dust and crumbs attract pests, and anything put away damp can develop mould, especially in a closed space. Fridges and freezers should be defrosted and dried with the doors left slightly open. Washing machines should be drained.

• Same-size sturdy boxes. Matching sizes stack into stable walls. Supermarket boxes of all shapes do not.
  • Small boxes for heavy things. Books, files and tins go in small boxes so each one can still be lifted safely.
  • Plastic crates with lids for anything you want extra protection for, such as documents or textiles.
  • Breathable dust sheets for furniture. Plastic sheeting wrapped tight can trap moisture.
  • Packing paper, bubble wrap and tape, plus a thick marker pen.
  • Pallets or plastic bearers to lift boxes slightly off the floor, if you are storing for a long time.

Fill every box to the top. A half-empty box crushes when another is stacked on it, and that is how things get broken in storage. Fill gaps with towels, clothes or scrunched paper.

Heavy items go at the bottom of each box, light ones at the top. Plates stand on their edges like records, wrapped individually. Glasses get a sheet of paper each and go upright. Lampshades and hats go in their own boxes with nothing on top.

Keep any box under a weight you can lift comfortably to shoulder height. If you cannot lift it, neither can whoever helps you get it out again.

sections.h2: Label for the person who unpacks
sections.html:
Write on at least two sides of every box, not the top, because the top disappears once it is stacked. Include the room it came from and a short list of contents. A number helps too.

Then keep a simple inventory: box number, contents, and roughly where in the unit it is. A note on your phone is enough. Photos of each open box before you seal it take seconds and save a lot of guessing later. The inventory also helps if you ever need to make an insurance claim, which our storage insurance guide covers.

1. Protect the floor layerPut pallets or bearers down first if you are storing long term, especially for boxes of paper or fabric.
  2. Large furniture against the back wallWardrobes, bookcases and mattresses on their sides go in first. Stand mattresses upright in covers rather than laying things on them.
  3. Build walls of boxesHeaviest boxes at the bottom, lighter ones higher. Keep each column straight and stable. Do not stack above a height you can safely reach.
  4. Leave an aisleA walkway down the middle or along one side lets you reach every wall. It costs some space but saves unloading everything for one box.
  5. Fill the gapsUse the spaces inside wardrobes and drawers for light items, cushions and linen.
  6. Front row for things you needSeasonal bags, the toolbox, paperwork and anything you will want back soon go last, nearest the door.

Take legs off tables and beds where you can and tape the fixings in a bag to the main piece. Keep sofas upright on their feet, not on end, unless the manufacturer says otherwise. Mirrors and pictures should stand on edge, wrapped, never flat with things on top. Our furniture storage guide goes into more detail.

Bikes can hang or lean along a wall. Garden tools are best grouped in a bin or crate so blades are covered. Anything with a fuel tank, such as a lawnmower, must be emptied first. Some things should not go in at all, and what not to store lists them.

sections.h2: Protecting against damp, dust and pests
sections.html:
Any closed space can collect dust, and anything stored damp will stay damp. A few habits make a big difference over a long storage period.

  • Make sure everything is completely dry before it goes in, including tents, garden cushions and freshly washed bedding.
  • Keep a small gap between boxes and the walls so air can move around them.
  • Never store food, even sealed snacks. It is the quickest way to attract mice and insects.
  • Cover upholstered furniture and mattresses with breathable covers.
  • Use lidded crates for paper, photos and fabric, and lift them off the floor.
  • Do not seal electronics in airtight plastic bags. Wrap them in a soft cloth and pack them in their original boxes if you still have them.

Visit every few weeks if you are storing long term. A quick look and a lift of a few covers will spot a problem while it is still small.

sections.h2: Making the most of our units
sections.html:
Our ground-floor units are windowless but have lighting and power already connected, so you can see what you are doing at any hour. With 24-hour access you can load in stages rather than cramming it all into one rushed day. The 150 sq ft and 180 sq ft units have roller shutters, which make loading furniture much easier. The 160 sq ft unit has a security door, so plan for items that go through a standard doorway.

If you are still choosing, our unit size guide helps you match your list to a space.

sections.h2: Keeping it organised after the first day
sections.html:
Units tend to start tidy and slide into chaos. Each visit, someone pulls out a box from the middle, takes what they need and leaves it by the door. Six months later, the aisle has gone.

A few rules keep it under control. Put boxes back where they came from, and update your inventory if you move something. Keep a small empty area near the door as a landing spot so you are not tempted to block the walkway. If the unit gets steadily fuller, that is a sign either to have a clear-out or to ask about a bigger space.

For businesses, the same applies with more urgency. Wasted time searching for stock is a real cost. Shelving with labelled bays, and a simple rule that every item has a home, pays for itself quickly.

faqs: Should I use plastic boxes or cardboard?

Both work. Cardboard is cheap and stacks well when the boxes match. Lidded plastic crates cost more but protect better against dust and damp, so they are worth it for paperwork, textiles and anything precious.
Can I wrap furniture in cling film?
It is fine for short moves, but for longer storage it can trap moisture against wood and fabric. Breathable dust sheets or blankets are safer.
How high can I stack?
Only as high as you can reach safely and the stack stays stable. Heavy boxes always go lowest.
Do I have to load everything in one go?
No. With 24-hour access you can take things over in several trips, which often makes for a tidier, better-organised unit.

pages.title: Storage When Moving House in Blackpool | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: Moving house in Blackpool and dates don't line up? How to use short-term storage between homes, when downsizing, or to stage a house sale.
pages.lead: House moves rarely go to plan. Completion slips, a chain breaks, or the new place needs work first. Short-term storage gives your belongings somewhere safe to wait while the dates sort themselves out.

sections.h2: When storage helps during a move
sections.html:
• A gap between completions. You have to leave one home before you can get into the next, and you are staying with family or renting short term.
  • Selling first. You are selling before buying so you can move quickly, and need somewhere for your things in the meantime.
  • Staging for viewings. Clearing out a third of the furniture makes rooms look bigger in photos and on viewings.
  • Downsizing. The new place is smaller and you have not decided what to keep, sell or give away.
  • Work on the new home. You want floors, decorating or a new kitchen done before the furniture arrives.

sections.h2: Plan around a timeline that will move
sections.html:
The safest assumption is that your dates will change at least once. Book storage that does not tie you in. Our terms are rolling monthly with a minimum of one month, then one month's notice to leave, so if completion slips by three weeks you are not stuck with a long contract.

Units at The Rock Factory are available from 1 November 2026, and if you pre-book, the first week is free. If your move is planned for late autumn or winter, it is worth booking early so the space is ready before you need it.

Think about the order things will come out, too. If you will be living out of a suitcase at a relative's for six weeks, pack the things you will want during that time separately and put them at the front of the unit.

Using storage between homes usually means moving twice: old house to unit, then unit to new house. That doubles the lifting, so it pays to make the second move easy.

  • Label boxes by the room they will go to in the new house, if you know the layout.
  • Load the unit so the things you need first in the new home come out first.
  • Keep bed parts, the kettle and a box of essentials together and easy to reach.
  • If you are hiring a removal firm, tell them up front that it is a two-stage move so they can plan the load.

Our guide to packing a storage unit covers loading order in detail.

sections.h2: Choosing a size for a household
sections.html:
For a whole home, most people look at our roller-shutter units because furniture goes straight in from the vehicle. The 150 sq ft unit at £65 a week often takes a two-bedroom home. The 180 sq ft unit at £78 a week gives more room for a larger household or for a walkway. For bigger homes, the 300 sq ft two-storey unit at £130 a week, or two adjoining units with an interconnecting door, may suit better.

If you are only storing the overflow while you stage a house for sale, a smaller space may do. Our storage pods and rooms open in spring 2027 at guide prices from £10 a week, though they are upstairs, so they suit boxes rather than sofas. The size guide has more detail.

Downsizing often means deciding about furniture and belongings that carry decades of memories. Doing that in the last fortnight before a move is stressful and leads to regret, either from keeping too much or letting go of something you wanted.

A unit lets you separate the move from the decisions. Take what fits into the new home, store the rest, and sort through it over a few weeks or months once you are settled. You will have a much clearer idea of what the new space can hold once you are living in it.

Set yourself a review date so storage does not drift on for years. Our decluttering guide has a simple method for that.

sections.h2: What to keep with you, not in storage
sections.html:
Some things are best carried with you during a move, even if there is space in the unit.

  • Passports, birth certificates, deeds and the paperwork for your sale or purchase.
  • Medicines, glasses and anything you need daily.
  • Jewellery, cash and small items of high value.
  • Laptops, chargers and the hard drive with your photos.
  • Keys for the old and new homes, and for the unit padlock.
  • Food, plants and pets. None of these belong in a storage unit.

Our list of what not to store covers the full set of banned and risky items.

sections.h2: Working out what the gap will cost
sections.html:
Because terms are monthly, it is easy to cost a move in advance. Taking our weekly prices over a year and dividing by twelve, the 150 sq ft unit at £65 a week works out at about £282 a month, and the 180 sq ft unit at £78 a week about £338 a month. A two-month gap in the 150 would cost about £563, with the first week free if you pre-booked.

Remember the deposit too. It equals one month's rent and is paid at the start along with the first month in advance, so you need that sum available on the day you move in.

Weigh that against the alternatives: a larger removal van kept for longer, paying a removal firm to hold goods, or squeezing everything into a relative's garage. Our storage unit vs garage comparison looks at that trade-off more closely.

1. Bring your paperworkTo start renting you will need one month's rent in advance, a security deposit equal to one month's rent, valid government-issued photo ID and a signed Direct Debit mandate. Sort this before moving day so loading is not held up.
  2. Bring a padlockA good-quality padlock is worth the money. Our security tips page explains what to look for.
  3. Load big items firstFurniture to the back, boxes in stable stacks, essentials at the front.
  4. Photograph the layoutA quick photo of the loaded unit helps you remember where things went.
  5. Check your insuranceAsk your home contents insurer whether goods in storage are covered while you are between homes.

See storage security tips and the storage insurance guide for more.

faqs: How short can I rent for?
The minimum term is one month. After that it rolls monthly and you give one month's notice when you want to leave.
Can I get to my things during the move?
Yes. There is 24-hour access, so you can collect something at the weekend or late in the evening.
Is my furniture insured in the unit?

Can I have post sent to the unit while I am between homes?

What if the new house is bigger than expected and I want it all back early?
Give one month's notice once your minimum month is up. You can also swap to a smaller unit for whatever is left.

pages.title: Storage During a Renovation | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: Renovating in Blackpool? How to clear rooms for builders, protect furniture from dust and choose storage that flexes when the job overruns.
pages.lead: Builders work faster in empty rooms, and your furniture lasts longer away from plaster dust. Here is how to plan storage around a renovation, from a single room to the whole house.

sections.h2: Why clearing rooms is worth it
sections.html:
It is tempting to shove everything into the room next door and throw a sheet over it. That works for a weekend of painting. For anything bigger, it causes problems.

  • Dust gets everywhere. Fine dust from sanding, plastering and cutting travels through the whole house, into drawers, fabrics and electronics.
  • Trades need room. Electricians need to reach sockets and floor voids. Floor fitters need empty floors. Every hour spent moving your things is an hour you are paying for.
  • Accidents happen. Ladders, dropped tools and wet paint are not kind to furniture.
  • You still have to live there. Piling two rooms into one leaves you with no usable space at all.

A short conversation before work starts saves a lot of hassle. Ask which rooms need to be completely empty, which can have furniture pushed to one side, and whether any floors or walls will be opened up. Ask too where they plan to put their own tools and materials, because that space often comes out of your hallway or garage.

Some builders are happy to help move large items on the first day. Others will expect the rooms to be clear when they arrive. Knowing which one you have tells you how much of the moving you need to organise yourself.

sections.h2: Plan storage by phase, not all at once
sections.html:
Few renovations touch every room at the same time. Ask your builder for the order of work and plan storage around it.

  1. List the rooms and datesWrite down which rooms are affected in which weeks. Note anything that has to come out completely, such as a kitchen being ripped out.
  2. Separate the essentialsDecide what you need to keep living with: a bed, a kettle, work clothes, the school bags. Everything else is a candidate for storage.
  3. Move out the first waveClear the rooms for the first phase, plus anything fragile from the rest of the house.
  4. Rotate as work movesAs rooms finish, bring their contents back and send the next room's things out. Good labelling makes this simple.
  5. Move back in stagesBring things home once the dust has settled and the paint is fully dry, not the day the decorator leaves.

Renovations overrun. Materials arrive late, a wall turns out to need more work than expected, a trade gets delayed on another job. So do not book storage that ends the day your builder says they will finish.

Our rental terms are built for this. The minimum is one month, then it rolls monthly with one month's notice. If the job runs two weeks long, you simply carry on. If it finishes early, give notice and you are done after the notice period.

The full details are on our rental terms page.

sections.h2: How much space a renovation needs
sections.html:
A single-room project, such as a bedroom or living room, often fits in a fairly small space if you are not storing large furniture. Once our first-floor pods and rooms open in spring 2027, a 50 or 75 sq ft room (guide prices £22 and £28 a week) may be enough for boxed contents and a few smaller pieces you can carry upstairs.

For a kitchen refit, the volume of crockery, pans and food cupboards surprises people. Add the dining table and chairs and you are into unit territory. The 150 sq ft roller-shutter unit at £65 a week takes a lot, and the shutter makes it easy to load a table or dresser straight from a van.

Whole-house projects, such as rewires, new floors throughout or an extension that opens up the back of the house, often call for the 180 sq ft unit or the 300 sq ft two-storey unit. Our size guide goes into more detail.

sections.h2: Protecting things from dust and damage
sections.html:
Even with things in storage, some items stay at home. Protect them properly.

  • Wrap electronics you are keeping in dust sheets and unplug them while work is going on.
  • Seal cupboards and wardrobes you are not using with low-tack tape round the doors.
  • Take curtains and soft furnishings down. They hold dust for months.
  • Clean everything before it goes into storage. Dust packed into a box will still be there when you open it.

For things going into the unit, wipe down surfaces, let freshly painted items dry fully, and use breathable covers rather than plastic wrap for wood and upholstery.

sections.h2: Building storage into the renovation budget
sections.html:
Storage is easy to forget when you are pricing up a project, then it appears as an unplanned cost halfway through. Add it as a line in the budget from the start, alongside skip hire and contingency.

Using our weekly prices, the 150 sq ft unit at £65 a week is about £282 a month, and the 180 sq ft unit at £78 a week is about £338 a month. A three-month kitchen and dining room project in the 150 would be roughly £845 in rent, plus a security deposit equal to one month's rent at the start. A pre-booking gets the first week free.

Weigh that against the cost of damage. A ruined sofa, a scratched dining table or a television full of plaster dust can easily cost more to replace than a few months of storage. So can paying a trade to work around clutter for days on end.

sections.h2: Storing materials as well as furniture
sections.html:
Some homeowners buy flooring, tiles, sanitaryware or kitchen units ahead of time, often to catch a sale. Storing them in a unit keeps them out of the way of the work and safe from damage until fitting day.

Low-risk materials such as wood, boxed tiles, flat-packed units and dry goods are fine. Solvent-based paints and chemicals in bulk, fuel and gas cylinders are not allowed unless agreed in writing. Water-based emulsion in normal domestic quantities is a different thing, but if you are unsure about anything, ask before you bring it.

Contractors doing the work may want their own space too. Our trades storage ideas page explains how builders use units for tools and stock.

With 24-hour access, you can collect something in the evening after the trades have gone, or drop off another load before work. Lighting and power are already connected in every unit, so a late visit in winter is not a fumble in the dark.

Keep one box marked clearly for the things you might need: the spare duvet, the slow cooker, the winter coats. Put it right by the door. You will probably open it more than you expect.

If you would like to view a unit before the builders start, message us on WhatsApp and we will arrange a time.

faqs: Can I store new kitchen units before they are fitted?
Yes, boxed or flat-packed units are fine. Keep them flat or as the manufacturer recommends, off the floor where you can, and keep the delivery paperwork with you.
Can my builder access my unit?
You control who you give access to. If you share your padlock key with a contractor, make sure you trust them and keep a note of what is stored.
Can I store paint in the unit?
Bulk solvent-based paints and chemicals are not allowed unless agreed in writing. Ask us about anything else before bringing it in.
What happens if my renovation finishes early?
After the one-month minimum, give one month's notice and you can leave at the end of it.
Is there somewhere to work in the unit while my house is a building site?
Wi-Fi and power are connected, and the two-storey unit has an upstairs area with a window. If you are thinking of working there, tell us what you plan, as business use needs prior approval.

pages.title: Student Storage in Blackpool | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: Student summer storage in Blackpool: share a pod or unit with housemates, pack a room in an afternoon and keep costs low on monthly terms.
h1: for the summer and in between
pages.lead: If you study in Blackpool and go home for the summer, dragging a room's worth of stuff across the country and back is a pain. Storing it locally, and sharing the cost with housemates, is often simpler.

sections.html:
Student lets often end at the start of summer, and the next tenancy starts weeks or months later. In between, you have bedding, a desk lamp, books, kitchen kit, a bike and a growing pile of clothes. Taking it all home may mean several train journeys or begging a lift from a parent.

Storage means you leave with a suitcase and pick everything up again when you are back. It also helps if you are going abroad for a placement or a study year, moving between halls and a shared house, or finishing your course and not yet sure where you will be living next.

We do not set our dates by any college or university calendar. You book a start date that suits you and give notice when you are done.

sections.h2: How much space one student needs
sections.html:
A typical student room packs down to around ten to twenty boxes, a suitcase or two and perhaps a bike, a chair or a small set of drawers. That is the sort of load our first-floor storage pods are designed for. They open in spring 2027, with guide prices (to be confirmed) of:

Splitting a space is the easiest way to keep costs down. A whole house of students can sometimes fit into one unit and divide the bill. Our ground-floor units are available from 1 November 2026. A 150 sq ft unit at £65 a week split five ways is £13 each per week, and the roller shutter makes loading quick on the day everyone moves out.

sections.h2: Packing a student room in an afternoon
sections.html:
1. Get boxes earlyThe last week of term is when everyone wants boxes. Buy or collect them a week or two before.
  2. Sort into three pilesTake home, store, get rid of. Be ruthless with the third pile: chipped mugs, the broken lamp, the duvet you never liked.
  3. Clean the kitchen kitWash and dry pans, plates and the toaster. Crumbs and grease left over summer are unpleasant to open in autumn and attract pests.
  4. Vacuum-pack bedding and clothesCompression bags save a lot of space for duvets and winter coats.
  5. Label everythingYour name, the box contents and, if sharing, a colour. Write on the sides as well as the top.

Our full packing guide has more detail on boxes and loading order.

sections.h2: What not to leave over summer
sections.html:
• Food of any kind, including unopened packets and tins. It attracts pests.
  • Laptops, passports and anything you might need while you are away.
  • Aerosols and gas canisters, such as camping stoves, in bulk.
  • Anything damp, such as a wet tent from a summer festival.
  • Plants. They will not survive the summer in a closed space.

See what not to store in a storage unit for the full list.

sections.h2: Paying and terms, in plain English

To start renting you need one month's rent in advance, a security deposit equal to one month's rent, valid government-issued photo ID (a passport or driving licence) and a signed Direct Debit mandate. Our storage insurance guide explains what to ask.

Final-year students face a different problem. You may be leaving Blackpool with no fixed address yet: a job search, a graduate scheme starting in the autumn, a few months of travelling. Storage gives you a pause button. Keep the things worth keeping in one place while you work out where you are going next, then collect or arrange to move them once you know.

It is also a good moment to be honest about what is worth keeping. Cheap furniture, worn-out kitchen kit and three years of lecture notes may cost more to store than to replace. Sell, donate or recycle before you book, so you only pay to store what you will actually use again.

sections.h2: Getting back in when you return
sections.html:
There is 24-hour access, so if your train gets in late or your new tenancy starts on a Sunday, you can still collect your things. Lighting is connected in every unit, so you are not unpacking in the dark.

Plan the return trip as carefully as the drop-off. If friends are driving, coordinate so you collect together and share the van. If you are moving into a different house from the one you left, have the new address and access sorted before you empty the unit.

To check what will be available for your dates, message us on WhatsApp.

faqs: Do I need to be a student to book?
No. Anyone can rent, as long as they can provide valid photo ID, the first month's rent, the deposit and a signed Direct Debit mandate.
Can I store for less than a month?

Can my parents pay?

Can I store my bike?
Yes. Bikes are fine. Pods are upstairs, so if your bike is heavy, a ground-floor unit shared with housemates may be easier.

Spring 2027. Prices shown are guide prices and will be confirmed nearer the time. Ground-floor units are available from 1 November 2026.

pages.title: Furniture Storage in Blackpool | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: How to store furniture in Blackpool without damage: cleaning, dismantling, wrapping and stacking sofas, beds, wardrobes and wooden pieces.
h1: so it comes out as it went in
pages.lead: Furniture is bulky, heavy and easy to mark. A bit of preparation before it goes into storage protects the pieces you care about and lets you fit far more into the space.

sections.html:
Before you pay to store a piece, ask a blunt question: would you buy it again at today's price? A good solid wood table, a family heirloom or a quality sofa you will use in your next home is usually worth storing. Flat-pack that has already been assembled twice, a mattress near the end of its life or a chest of drawers you never liked often is not.

A rough way to decide is to compare the replacement cost with the share of rent the item takes up. A large wardrobe might take up a tenth of a 150 sq ft unit. At £65 a week that is roughly £28 a month of space. If you will store it for a year and could replace it for £150, it may not earn its place.

Our decluttering guide has more on making these decisions without regret.

sections.h2: Prepare each piece before it moves
sections.html:
Start with a clean. Vacuum sofas and chairs, including down the sides of cushions. Wipe wooden surfaces with a slightly damp cloth and let them dry fully. Empty every drawer, even if it is tempting to leave them full. Full drawers make pieces much heavier and can strain joints and runners when lifted.

Then photograph anything valuable, including existing marks or scratches. It gives you a record for insurance and a reminder of how things went together.

Taking furniture apart saves space and reduces the chance of damage. Bed frames, table legs, wardrobe doors and shelving all come apart more easily than people think.

  • Put every screw, bolt and fitting in a labelled sandwich bag and tape it firmly to the main piece.
  • Keep assembly instructions with the item, or photograph each stage as you take it apart.
  • Wrap legs together and label them with the piece they belong to.
  • Remove glass shelves and pack them separately, on edge, wrapped and padded.

Some antique or older pieces are glued rather than screwed, and forcing them apart can do real damage. If in doubt, leave them whole.

How you wrap depends on how long you are storing. For a short move, stretch wrap protects against knocks. For storage of more than a few weeks, breathable covers are safer, because plastic pressed against wood or fabric can trap moisture.

  • Wood: moving blankets or old duvets, held with tape on the blanket, not the wood.
  • Upholstery: breathable sofa and chair covers, or clean cotton sheets.
  • Mattresses: a proper mattress bag, stored flat or on its side as the maker recommends.
  • Leather: cotton covers, kept away from anything that could stain it.
  • Mirrors and glass: cardboard corners, bubble wrap and a marked "fragile, this side up" label.

1. Floor firstLay down pallets, boards or old rugs to keep items off the floor, especially if storing long term.
  2. Tall pieces at the backWardrobes, bookcases and dressers along the back and side walls.
  3. Sofas on their feetKeep sofas upright. Standing them on end can damage frames and springs. Place light items on top only if they cannot slip.
  4. Tables on their topsOnce legs are off, a table top can go on its edge against a wall, padded on both sides.
  5. Fill the voidsUse wardrobe and drawer space for cushions, curtains and linen.
  6. Leave an aisleEven a narrow walkway lets you check on things and get to them without moving everything.

For anything bulky, a roller shutter makes life far easier. You can reverse a van close to the door and carry a sofa straight in. Our 150 sq ft roller-shutter unit (£65 a week) and 180 sq ft roller-shutter unit (£78 a week) both have this.

The 160 sq ft unit (£69 a week) is reached by a security door. It works well for furniture that goes through a normal internal doorway, but measure wide items first.

The two-storey unit has a roller-shutter ground floor and an upstairs area reached by an internal staircase. Bulky furniture belongs downstairs. Our first-floor pods and rooms, opening spring 2027, are reached by stairs too, so they suit smaller pieces such as chairs, bedside tables and flat-pack.

sections.h2: Moving furniture safely on the day
sections.html:
Most furniture damage happens in transit, not in storage. Lift with two people for anything heavier than a dining chair. Carry tables upside down so the legs, or the leg fixings, are not knocked. Protect door frames as well as the furniture. Strap items inside the van so they cannot slide on corners.

At the unit, unload in the order you plan to stack: the big pieces that go to the back first, then boxes. If you have a lot of furniture, consider a removal firm, since experienced movers wrap and load quickly and are less likely to scrape a wall or a sideboard.

Visit every month or two if you are storing for a long time. Lift a cover or two, check for any marks or signs of pests, and make sure nothing has shifted. If a stack looks unstable, fix it before it falls.

Avoid putting heavy boxes on top of upholstered furniture. Over months, the weight can flatten cushions and leave permanent dents. If you need the space, put a sheet of board across first to spread the load.

When things come out, give wooden pieces a day or two to settle at home before polishing, and air upholstered pieces in a well-ventilated room.

sections.h2: Storing furniture you plan to sell or upcycle
sections.html:
Not all stored furniture is waiting to go back into a home. Some people collect pieces to restore and sell. If that is you, think about whether you want a pure storage unit or somewhere to work as well. Our furniture upcycling unit ideas page looks at that, including what is and is not permitted. All business use needs our prior approval.

If you are simply selling off a houseful after a move or bereavement, a unit gives buyers somewhere to view pieces without coming into your home. Keep the most saleable items near the door.

faqs: Can I store a sofa on its end to save space?
It is best not to. Standing a sofa on its end puts strain on the frame and springs. Keep it on its feet and use the space above for light boxes on a board.
Should I wrap wooden furniture in plastic?
Not for long-term storage. Plastic can trap moisture against wood. Use moving blankets, old duvets or breathable covers.
Will my wardrobe fit through the door?
Our units are quoted by floor area only. For very large items, choose a roller-shutter unit, and if a particular piece worries you, ask us on WhatsApp before booking.
Can I store white goods with furniture?
Yes, but defrost and dry fridges and freezers completely and leave the doors slightly open. Drain washing machines first.
Can I come and check on my furniture whenever I like?
Yes. There is 24-hour access, and you can also view the CCTV covering the entrance and the area outside the units on a free app.

pages.title: Document and Archive Storage | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: Storing business records and archives in Blackpool: boxing, indexing and protecting paperwork, plus pointers to HMRC and ICO guidance.
pages.lead: Paper records pile up fast, and many have to be kept for years. A tidy, well-indexed archive in a secure unit frees up your office or home while keeping everything you are required to hold within reach.

sections.h2: Why you are keeping these records
sections.html:
Before boxing anything, be clear about why each set of papers exists. Most business archives fall into a few groups:

  • Tax and accounting records that HMRC may ask to see, such as invoices, receipts, bank statements and payroll records.
  • Company records a limited company is required to keep, such as minutes and registers.
  • Customer and staff files that contain personal data and fall under data protection law.
  • Contracts, warranties and property papers you may need if a dispute arises.
  • History and sentiment: old catalogues, photos, founding documents. Not required, but valued.

Each group has a different reason for being kept, and so a different point at which it can safely be destroyed.

HMRC sets minimum periods for keeping tax records, and they vary depending on whether you are self-employed, a limited company or an employer. As an example, GOV.UK says limited companies must generally keep accounting records for six years from the end of the last company financial year they relate to, and longer in some circumstances. Self-employed people have their own rules, set out on GOV.UK.

Data protection works the other way. Under UK GDPR's storage limitation principle, explained by the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), you should not keep personal data for longer than you need it. That means an archive should have a plan for destroying records as well as keeping them.

These rules change and depend on your situation, so check the official guidance listed at the bottom of this page, or ask your accountant, before you decide what to keep or shred.

A retention schedule sounds formal, but for a small business it can be a single page. List each type of record, how long you keep it, why, and what happens at the end.

Record typeKeep untilThen
Sales and purchase invoicesEnd of the period HMRC requiresShred securely
Former staff filesOnly as long as you have a clear reasonShred securely
Old customer enquiriesOnly as long as neededShred securely
Company historyIndefinitely, by choiceReview every few years

Write the destroy-by date on the side of each box. When you visit the unit, anything past its date goes out for shredding. This stops the archive growing forever, which is both a cost and, for personal data, a risk.

1. Use proper archive boxesStandard-size boxes with lids stack neatly and can be lifted when full. Lidded plastic crates add protection against dust and damp.
  2. One subject and one year per boxDo not mix years. When a year's records reach their destroy date, the whole box goes.
  3. Number every boxMark the number, subject, date range and destroy-by date on two sides.
  4. Keep an indexA spreadsheet listing box numbers and contents lets you find any file in minutes. Keep a copy off-site.
  5. Shelve, do not stack highSteel shelving keeps boxes off the floor and lets you pull one out without moving ten others.

If boxes contain personal data, you are responsible for keeping them secure wherever they are. The ICO's guidance on security says organisations should take appropriate measures to protect personal data, and that covers paper as well as digital records.

  • Use a strong padlock and limit who has the key.
  • Do not label boxes with sensitive details, such as a client's name and "medical". Use box numbers and keep the meaning in your index.
  • Keep a log of who visits the unit and what they remove.
  • Shred securely at the end of the retention period, rather than putting papers in general waste.

Our units have 24-hour access and you can view CCTV covering the entrance and the area outside the units on a free app. Those help, but they are not a substitute for your own controls. The storage security tips page has more.

sections.h2: Protecting paper from damp and pests
sections.html:
Paper is vulnerable to moisture, so keep it off the floor on shelving or pallets and away from walls. Lidded crates are worth the cost for anything important. Do not store paper alongside anything that might leak, such as liquids or white goods that have not been fully dried.

Never store food in an archive unit. Mice and insects will happily eat cardboard and paper once they have been drawn in. Visit regularly and look for any signs of damage early.

Scanning is worth considering for records you consult often. A digital copy means you rarely need to visit the unit, and the paper original stays undisturbed. Check the HMRC guidance on whether digital copies are acceptable for the records you hold.

Archives are not only a business problem. Households collect decades of bank statements, payslips, old tax returns, property paperwork and letters. GOV.UK gives guidance on how long individuals should keep pay and tax records, and it is generally far shorter than the time most people actually hold on to them.

A useful split is three-way. Keep originals that are hard to replace, such as deeds, wills, birth and marriage certificates, somewhere secure and accessible, which for most people means at home or with a solicitor rather than in a unit. Keep recent financial records you might need for a few years in labelled boxes. Shred the rest securely.

Family history, photos and letters are a different matter. They are not required by anyone, but they are irreplaceable. Store them in lidded crates, off the floor, and consider scanning the most precious items so a copy exists elsewhere.

For a handful of boxes, one of our first-floor pods (opening spring 2027, guide prices from £10 a week) may be enough, as long as you are happy to carry boxes up stairs. For a larger archive, a ground-floor unit with shelving works well. The 160 sq ft security-door unit at £69 a week suits archives in particular, since boxes go through a standard door and you do not need a shutter.

If you also want a desk to work through files, the two-storey unit gives you storage below and an upstairs area with a window. Lighting, power and Wi-Fi are connected in every unit. Business use needs our prior approval, so mention what you plan when you message us on WhatsApp.

faqs: Can I keep my business archive in a storage unit?
Yes. Many businesses do. Make sure you can still produce records when HMRC or anyone else is entitled to see them, which is where a good index helps.
Do I have to keep paper copies?
Not always. HMRC accepts records in various forms in many cases, but check GOV.UK for the records you keep before relying on scans alone.
Is my archive insured?

No insurance is included. Check your business insurance policy covers documents held off-site, and think about the cost of recreating records, not just the boxes. Our storage insurance guide explains what to ask.
Can I shred documents at the unit?
Shredding small amounts by hand is no different from any other office task. If you are thinking of setting up a shredding business, talk to us first, as all business use needs prior approval.
Can I get to a file at short notice?
Yes. There is 24-hour access, so a late-night search for an old invoice is possible.

h1: for a town that runs on seasons
pages.lead: Blackpool's year has a strong rhythm, from the busy summer to the autumn Illuminations and a quieter winter. Seasonal storage lets households and businesses keep what they need now and park the rest.

sections.html:
Few places swing between seasons quite like a seaside resort. Through the warmer months, the town fills with visitors. Autumn brings the Illuminations, which extend the season for many local businesses. Then winter is quieter, and many people turn to repairs, refits and planning for next year.

That rhythm affects what people need to store. A guest house owner might need room for spare bedding and garden furniture in winter. A market trader might need more stock space ahead of the busy months. A family might want the paddling pool and barbecue out of the shed in October, and the Christmas tree out of the loft in November.

Most homes have two sets of things: what you use now, and what you will use in six months. Keeping both at home means cupboards that never close and a garage you cannot get into.

Camping kit and beach gearChristmas decorations and the artificial tree

Businesses that trade with visitors often need very different amounts of space through the year. Stock builds up before the busy months, then dwindles. Equipment used only in summer sits idle all winter.

  • Market and event traders: gazebos, tables, display stands and stock between events.

sections.h2: Winter refits for guest houses and holiday lets

The quieter months are when many accommodation owners redecorate, replace carpets or refit bathrooms. Clearing rooms of beds, wardrobes and soft furnishings while the work goes on keeps everything clean and lets trades work faster.

A roller-shutter unit suits this best because beds, mattresses and wardrobes load straight in. sections.h2: Packing seasonal items so they last

  2. Remove fuel and gasEmpty lawnmowers and generators of fuel. Gas cylinders from barbecues and patio heaters must not be stored in bulk unless agreed in writing.

pages.title: Declutter With Storage, Not Into It | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: How to use a storage unit to declutter your Blackpool home properly: sort, store for a set time, then decide, so it doesn't become a dumping ground.
pages.lead: Used well, a storage unit is a breathing space that helps you decide what to keep. Used badly, it is a monthly bill for things you have forgotten. This guide is about the first kind.

sections.html:
Storage companies do not often say this, but it is true: some people would be better off not renting storage at all. If a unit becomes a place where things go so you never have to think about them, you end up paying every month for a problem you have just moved down the road.

The aim of this guide is the opposite. Storage, with a clear plan and a deadline, can make decluttering easier, because it removes the pressure of deciding everything at once. You get your space back now and make the hard calls over weeks rather than in one exhausting weekend.

sections.h2: When storage genuinely helps you declutter
sections.html:
• You have inherited a household's contents and are not ready to decide.
  • You want to see how a room feels without certain furniture before you sell it.
  • You are sorting a family home with siblings who live elsewhere and need time to agree who wants what.
  • You are preparing to sell items in batches and want them out of the house in the meantime.
  • You are working through years of paperwork and need somewhere to spread it out.

In each case, storage is temporary and has a clear end point. That is what makes it worth paying for.

Work through one room or one cupboard at a time. Every item goes into one of four piles, and nothing goes back on the shelf until it has been sorted.

  1. Keep at homeThings you use regularly or truly love having around you.
  2. Sell or donateGood-condition items you do not need. Photograph them and list them straight away, while you have the energy.
  3. Recycle or binBroken, worn out or unwanted by anyone. Get it out of the house the same week.
  4. Store to decideItems you are genuinely unsure about. These go into storage with a date on the box.

The fourth pile should be the smallest. If it is the biggest, you are postponing rather than decluttering.

sections.h2: Set a deadline before you book
sections.html:
Before anything goes into storage, write down a review date. Three months is a good default. Six months makes sense for seasonal items you want to see through a full cycle. Put the date in your phone calendar.

On that date, go to the unit and look at each "store to decide" box. If you have not missed it or thought about it, that is your answer. Sell, donate or recycle it. If you have been missing it, take it home.

Our terms make this easy to stick to. The minimum is one month, then rolling monthly, with one month's notice to leave. No long lease means no reason to keep paying once the job is done.

Be clear about the cost so you can compare it with what the items are worth. Our first-floor pods, opening spring 2027, have guide prices from £10 a week for 15 sq ft, about £43 a month. The 25 sq ft pod at a guide price of £14 a week is about £61 a month. A 50 sq ft room at a guide price of £22 a week is about £95 a month.

If you are clearing a whole house of furniture, a ground-floor unit is more realistic. The 150 sq ft unit at £65 a week is about £282 a month.

Over three months, a 25 sq ft pod would be roughly £182. If the things inside are worth less than that to you, it may be kinder to your wallet to let them go now.

If you are not sure where to start, these are the places that tend to hold the most for the least use:

  • The loft: old toys, boxes from the last move, and things kept "just in case".
  • The garage: half-finished projects, spare furniture and tools you own two of.
  • The spare room: often a storage room with a bed in it.
  • Under the stairs: sports kit, vacuum cleaners and bags of bags.
  • Wardrobes: clothes that do not fit, or that you have not worn in two years.

Start with the room that annoys you most. A visible win early on keeps you going.

If you are selling in batches, a unit can act as a holding area. Keep the items you are listing near the front and photograph them where they are. Once the deal is agreed, meet buyers somewhere sensible or arrange collection so they are not wandering around the site. Some people find it simpler to bring items home just before collection.

If selling becomes a regular thing, perhaps at markets or online, you may be running a small business. Our guide to selling at Blackpool markets and ideas for online sellers may help. Business use of a unit needs our prior approval.

sections.h2: Keeping the space once you have it
sections.html:
Decluttering does not stay done on its own. A few habits help: one in, one out for clothes and books; a box by the front door for things to donate, taken away when full; and a once-a-year look at the loft or garage.

If you find you still need regular overflow space for seasonal items after the clear-out, that is a different, more deliberate use of storage. Our seasonal storage guide explains how to rotate summer and winter kit, and the storage unit vs garage comparison helps you work out whether paying for space makes sense.

Clearing a loved one's home is one of the hardest decluttering jobs there is. It often comes with a deadline, such as the end of a tenancy or a house sale, and with grief that makes every decision heavier.

A unit can take the time pressure off. Move the contents somewhere safe, hand back the keys, and sort through it when you and your family are ready. Keep photos, letters and small treasures somewhere dry and in lidded crates. Make a list of who has asked for what, and keep it with the boxes.

If you would like to talk through what space might suit, message us on WhatsApp. There is no pressure to book.

faqs: How long should I store things while decluttering?
Set a review date before you start. Three months suits most household clear-outs. Six months suits items you want to see through a full season.
What if I never get round to sorting the unit?
That is the trap to avoid. Put the review date in your calendar, and if you keep missing it, ask a friend to come with you. Monthly terms mean you can stop paying as soon as you are done.
Can I sell items directly from my unit?
You can store items you are selling. Running a regular selling business from the unit needs prior approval, so tell us what you have in mind.
Is a pod enough for decluttering?
Often, yes. The "store to decide" pile should be small. Pods open in spring 2027 at guide prices from £10 a week.

pages.title: What Not to Store in a Storage Unit | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: What you can't or shouldn't keep in a storage unit in Blackpool: banned items, fuel and gas, food, cars and valuables, with the reasons why.
h1: in a storage unit, and why
pages.lead: Most things are fine in storage. A few are banned outright, some are only allowed with written agreement, and others are allowed but a bad idea. Knowing which is which keeps you, your belongings and everyone else in the building safe.

sections.h2: Why there are rules at all
sections.html:
A storage building is shared. Your unit sits next to someone else's furniture, a small business's stock and another person's family photos. One unsafe item can put all of it at risk, through fire, leaks, fumes or pests.

Rules also come from the buildings insurance. Insurers set conditions about what a building can hold and what activities can happen in it. If those conditions are broken, cover can be affected for everyone. That is why some of our rules may seem strict for the item in question. They protect the whole building.

sections.h2: Not permitted at The Rock Factory
sections.html:
• Cars. Car storage is not permitted because of the buildings insurance.
  • Bulk flammable liquids and gases, such as fuel, solvent-based paints and chemicals, and gas cylinders, unless we have agreed it in writing.
  • Melting or heating combustible materials, such as waxes, plastics, resins and oils. That rules out activities like candle and soap making, resin casting and 3D print farms.
  • Cooking and hot food.

Low-risk materials such as wood, paper, card, fabric and dry goods are fine. All business use needs our prior approval, so tell us what you plan to store and do before you move in.

sections.h2: Things no storage unit should hold
sections.html:
Beyond our own rules, some things should never go into any storage unit:

  • Anything illegal, stolen or that you are not entitled to possess.
  • Explosives, fireworks, ammunition and firearms.
  • Toxic, corrosive or hazardous substances and waste, including asbestos.
  • Anything living: people, pets, plants.
  • Anything that smells strongly, leaks or gives off fumes.

Storage units are also not designed for anyone to live or sleep in, so do not plan to use one that way, even for a night.

Food is the most common mistake. It does not have to be fresh to cause a problem. Dried pasta, cereal, pet food and biscuits all attract mice and insects, and once pests arrive, they move between units and chew through cardboard, fabric and wiring.

So leave all food out, including unopened packets and tins. Wash kitchen equipment before packing it so crumbs and grease do not linger. Clear out the cupboards of any furniture you are storing, such as dressers and sideboards.

Businesses storing food stock are a separate case and would need to talk to us first. The Food Standards Agency has guidance for food businesses on safe storage, and cooking or hot food is not permitted at our units.

Lawnmowers, strimmers, generators and pressure washers are fine as long as they are empty of fuel. Run them dry or drain the tank, and let them air before storing. Keep spare fuel cans at home or dispose of the fuel properly. Bulk fuel is not allowed unless agreed in writing.

Barbecues and patio heaters should go in without their gas cylinders. E-bikes and electric scooters are allowed as normal items, but it is good practice to store them with the battery at a moderate charge, not charging, and to remove the battery if the maker suggests it.

Tradespeople storing tools and materials will find our trades storage ideas useful.

Most homes have a cupboard of bleach, polish, aerosols, weedkiller and old tins of this and that. These are easy to sweep into a box on moving day without thinking. Try not to.

  • Keep household chemicals at home where you can, or use them up or dispose of them properly before you move.
  • Never pack chemicals in the same box as fabric, paper or food-related items.
  • Check old tins and bottles for leaks or bulging. Damaged containers should go to a household waste recycling centre, not into storage.
  • Take loose batteries out of toys, torches and decorations, as they can leak over time.
  • Store power-tool batteries separately from the tools, away from metal objects that could short the terminals.

Remember that solvent-based paints and chemicals in bulk are not allowed unless agreed in writing. If your list includes anything you are unsure about, check with us first.

Some things are permitted but are better kept elsewhere.

  • Cash, jewellery and small valuables. These are easy to carry and hard to replace. Keep them at home in a safe or at a bank.
  • Passports and key personal documents. You may need them at short notice.
  • The only copy of anything. Photos, hard drives and family papers should have a copy somewhere else.
  • Medicines. They can degrade, and you may need them.
  • Delicate instruments and artwork. Possible with care, but think about temperature and humidity in any closed space, and talk to a specialist about very valuable pieces.

Our units have no climate control, so anything sensitive to cold or damp needs extra thought. Lidded crates, breathable covers and keeping things off the floor all help, as the packing guide explains.

sections.h2: Business activities as well as items
sections.html:
Our rules cover what you do in a unit as well as what you keep there. Making candles, soap or resin pieces involves heating combustible materials, which is not allowed. Running banks of 3D printers is not allowed either. Equipment that needs three-phase power will not work, as units have standard single-phase electricity only.

Many crafts and trades are fine, and our ideas for makers and studios page has examples. Our health and safety guide for small units covers the basics of working safely. If you are unsure whether something is allowed, message us on WhatsApp before you sign.

sections.h2: A quick check before you load
sections.html:
Before the van leaves, run through five questions for anything you are unsure about. Could it catch fire, leak or give off fumes? Could it attract pests? Is it alive? Is it something you might need urgently? Is it irreplaceable?

A yes to any of the first three means it stays out. A yes to either of the last two means it is probably better kept at home. Everything else can go in, packed properly. It takes a couple of minutes and saves real problems later.

faqs: Can I store a motorbike?
Car storage is not permitted. For motorbikes and other vehicles, ask us before booking, and make sure any vehicle has no fuel in it if it is agreed.
Can I store tins of paint?
Bulk solvent-based paints are not allowed unless agreed in writing. Ask us about small domestic quantities of other paints before bringing them in.
Can I store a camping gas stove?
The stove is fine. Gas cylinders and canisters in bulk are not, unless agreed in writing. Remove them and keep them elsewhere.
Can I store wood and timber?
Yes. Wood, paper, card, fabric and dry goods are classed as low-risk materials and are fine.
Can I store a fridge or freezer?
Yes, once it is defrosted, cleaned and fully dry. Leave the door slightly open to stop mould and smells.
What happens if someone stores something banned?
It puts the building, other tenants and the insurance at risk. If you are unsure about any item, ask before you bring it in rather than after.
sources: Food safety and hygiene for businesses (Food Standards Agency)

pages.title: Storage Unit Security Tips | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: Simple storage unit security tips for Blackpool renters: choosing a padlock, keeping an inventory, managing keys and using the CCTV app.
h1: simple habits that make a difference
pages.lead: Good security is mostly about habits rather than gadgets. A decent padlock, a clear inventory and a little discretion protect your things far better than you might expect.

sections.html:
It is worth being clear about what is in place at The Rock Factory and what is down to you. Every tenant gets free app access to CCTV covering the entrance and the area outside the units, so you can check on things from your phone. There is 24-hour access, which means you can visit whenever you need, and lighting is connected in every unit.

Inside your unit, security is in your hands. You choose and fit the padlock, decide who has a key, and decide what goes in. The rest of this guide is about doing that well.

Think of it as two layers: the building's shared measures outside, and your own choices on the other side of the door.

The padlock is the single most important thing you buy. It is worth spending a little more.

  • Closed or shrouded shackle. A padlock where little of the shackle is exposed is much harder to cut with bolt cutters.
  • Hardened steel body and shackle. Cheap brass padlocks are easy to break.
  • Disc-style padlocks are popular for storage because their shape leaves almost nothing to grip.
  • Security rating. Look for an independent security grading on the packaging. Higher grades take longer to defeat.
  • Size that fits. Check the shackle fits your shutter or door fitting without a lot of free play.

Weather and grit can stiffen any lock. A squirt of lock lubricant every few months keeps it working smoothly.

Every spare key is a way in. Keep track of yours.

  • Keep the spare at home, not on the same keyring as your car or house keys.
  • Know exactly who has a copy. Write it down if more than two people do.
  • If you use a combination lock, change the code from the factory default, do not use birthdays, and change it when someone no longer needs access.
  • If a key is lost, replace the padlock straight away rather than hoping it turns up.

When you share a unit with housemates, a business partner or family, agree access rules at the start. It avoids awkward conversations later.

sections.h2: A little discretion goes a long way
sections.html:
Thieves look for easy, valuable targets. Do not give them a reason to pick yours.

  • Keep the door or shutter closed while you work inside if you are storing tools or high-value stock.
  • Use plain boxes rather than the original packaging for televisions, power tools and electronics.
  • Do not post photos online that show the inside of your unit and its contents.
  • Close and lock up every time, even if you are popping to your vehicle for a minute.

The best security for some things is not storing them at all. Cash, jewellery, passports and anything irreplaceable are safer at home, in a safe or with a bank. The same goes for the only copy of photos or important files. Keep backups somewhere separate.

Our list of what not to store goes through the rest, and the document and archive guide explains how to protect paperwork that contains personal data.

An inventory is useful for finding things, and essential if something ever goes wrong. It need not be complicated.

  1. Number your boxesWrite the number on two sides.
  2. List the contentsA simple note on your phone or a spreadsheet: box number, contents, rough value for anything worth more than a few pounds.
  3. Photograph valuable itemsInclude serial numbers for tools and electronics.
  4. Photograph the unitTake a photo of the loaded unit each time you make a big change.
  5. Keep a copy off-siteStore the list in cloud storage or email it to yourself.

Insurers often ask for proof of what was stored. Our storage insurance guide explains why this matters.

sections.h2: Visit, check and use the app
sections.html:
Units that are visited regularly are less likely to have a problem go unnoticed. With 24-hour access, a quick check fits round any schedule. Look at the padlock, make sure nothing has been moved, and look for any signs of damp or pests at the same time.

Use the CCTV app between visits, especially if you are away for a while. If you see anything that worries you, tell us and, if a crime has happened, report it to the police.

sections.h2: Security is about more than theft
sections.html:
Most losses in storage are not break-ins. They are damp boxes, chewed cardboard, a stack that toppled, or something forgotten and never found again. Treat these as part of security too.

  • Never store food, which brings in pests that can move between units.
  • Keep boxes off the floor on pallets or shelving, and away from walls.
  • Stack heavy boxes low and keep stacks stable.
  • Check your stored items regularly, not just the lock.

The packing guide has more on loading safely.

If you store stock, tools or records for a business, a few extra habits help. Keep a log of who visits and what they take. Limit keys to the people who need them. Do a stock check from time to time so you notice anything missing quickly. Check what your business insurance requires, as some policies specify the type of lock or how goods must be stored.

For businesses choosing between unit types, the 160 sq ft unit has a personnel security door rather than a roller shutter, and some units have interconnecting doors so you can combine shutter and personnel-door access. Ask about the options when you message us on WhatsApp.

Security matters at the end of a rental as well as the start. Check every corner of the unit before you hand it back, as small boxes and loose items are easy to miss in poor light. Take your padlock with you. If you used a combination lock, change the code before you use it elsewhere.

Update your inventory and your insurer if your goods are moving to a new address. And if anyone else had access to the unit, let them know you have left, so nobody turns up later expecting to find their things there.

faqs: Do you provide a padlock?
You provide your own padlock, so you hold the only keys. Choose a good-quality one with a closed or shrouded shackle.
What does the CCTV cover?
The CCTV covers the entrance and the area outside the units. Tenants get free app access to view it.
Can someone else collect things from my unit?
If you give them your key or code, yes. Only share access with people you trust, and keep a note of who has it.
Should I tell my insurer how my unit is secured?
Yes, if they ask. Give accurate details: your own padlock, 24-hour access and CCTV covering the entrance and the area outside the units. Do not guess at features you are not sure about.
What should I do if I lose my padlock key?
Replace the padlock as soon as you can. If you cannot get into your unit, message us and we will talk you through the options.

pages.desc: Do you need insurance for a storage unit? Check your home contents policy, consider specialist storage cover and know what to ask. Blackpool guide.
h1: what to check before you load up
pages.lead: Insurance is not included with our units, and we do not sell it. This guide explains your main options in plain English and the questions worth asking, so you can arrange cover that suits what you store.

sections.h2: Why you need to think about it
sections.html:
When you rent a storage unit, the building has its own insurance, but that is about the building, not your belongings. If your things are damaged or stolen, you will usually need your own cover to claim for them.

At The Rock Factory, insurance for your goods is not included in the rent and we do not provide it. That is common in the storage world, but it does mean the job falls to you. The good news is that it is often straightforward.

sections.h2: Option one: your home contents policy
sections.html:
Many home contents policies include some cover for belongings kept away from home, sometimes including in storage. But the details vary a great deal between insurers and policies.

  • Does the policy cover goods in a storage unit at all, or only things temporarily away from home?
  • Is there a limit on the total value, often a percentage of your contents sum insured?
  • Is there a time limit, after which cover stops?
  • Are some items excluded, such as valuables, business goods or electronics?
  • Does theft cover require visible signs of forced entry?
  • Do you need to tell the insurer the address and what is stored?

Read the policy wording, then call or email your insurer and ask. Get the answer in writing if you can.

Moving house causes a common gap. If you have sold your home and not yet moved into the next one, your contents policy might be tied to the old address and may stop when you leave. Your new policy might not start until you move in.

If that applies to you, ask your insurer specifically about cover for goods in storage between addresses. Some insurers handle this easily. Others do not, and specialist storage insurance fills the gap. Our moving house guide covers the rest of the planning.

Specialist storage insurance is designed for goods kept in a self-storage unit. It is usually priced on the value of what you store and is often sold monthly, which fits rolling storage terms.

When comparing policies, look at:

  • What events are covered: fire, flood, theft, accidental damage.
  • The excess you pay on any claim.
  • Single-item limits, which matter if you have one valuable piece.
  • Conditions on how goods must be stored, such as off the floor or in sealed boxes.
  • Whether it covers business stock, if you are a business.

Check that any insurer or broker you use is authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority. You can search the FCA's Financial Services Register online.

If you store business stock, tools or equipment, your business insurance is usually the right place for cover. Some policies cover stock at another location only if the insurer is told. Others need it added. Tools often have separate cover with its own conditions.

Our small business insurance guide looks at the main types of business cover, including public liability, which matters if customers or clients visit you at the unit.

sections.h2: Work out what it is all worth
sections.html:
Underinsuring is common. People guess the value of their stored goods and guess low. If you claim, the insurer may reduce the payout in proportion.

  1. List everythingGo box by box from your inventory.
  2. Value at replacement costAsk what it would cost to buy again, not what you paid years ago, if your policy is new-for-old.
  3. Note high-value itemsAnything over the policy's single-item limit may need to be listed separately.
  4. Keep evidenceReceipts, photos and serial numbers make any claim much smoother.
  5. Review itUpdate the value when you add or remove a lot from the unit.

Our storage security tips explain how to keep a simple inventory.

• Cover ending after a set period of goods being away from home, when storage carries on.
  • Business goods in a personal policy. Household policies often exclude stock, tools used for work or equipment.
  • No accidental damage cover, so a dropped television or a knocked mirror is not included.
  • A single-item limit lower than the value of your most expensive piece.
  • Not telling the insurer that goods are in storage, which can affect a claim later.

None of these is unusual, which is why it is worth a short phone call before you move in rather than finding out when you need to claim.

sections.h2: If you ever need to claim
sections.html:
1. Do not move things more than you need toTake photos of any damage exactly as you found it.
  2. Report a crimeIf anything has been stolen, report it to the police and note the crime reference number. Insurers usually ask for it.
  3. Tell usLet us know what has happened so we can check the building and help with any information we hold.
  4. Contact your insurer promptlyMost policies require you to report a claim within a set time.
  5. Send your evidenceYour inventory, photos, receipts and serial numbers will make the claim much easier.

sections.h2: Reducing the risk in the first place
sections.html:
Insurance is the safety net. Good habits make it less likely you will need it. Use a strong padlock, pack well, keep things off the floor, and leave out anything we do not allow, such as bulk flammable liquids or gas cylinders. Storing banned items could affect any claim as well as the building.

Keep the most valuable and irreplaceable things somewhere else entirely. Our page on what not to store explains what to leave out.

If an insurer asks you questions about the site that this page does not answer, message us on WhatsApp and we will tell you what we can.

faqs: Is insurance included in the rent?
No. Insurance for your goods is not included, and we do not provide it. You need to arrange your own cover.
Does my home insurance cover my storage unit?
It might. Many contents policies include some cover for goods away from home, but limits and conditions vary. Ask your insurer directly.
Do I need to show proof of insurance to rent?

To move in we ask for one month's rent in advance, a deposit equal to one month's rent, valid government-issued photo ID and a signed Direct Debit mandate. Arranging insurance is your decision, but we strongly suggest it.
What details might an insurer ask about the site?

Usually the address, the type of lock and access arrangements. Our address is The Old Rock Factory, Keswick Road (off Park Road), Blackpool FY1 5PB. Units have 24-hour access and there is CCTV covering the entrance and the area outside the units.
Does specialist storage insurance cost a lot?
It depends on the value of what you store and the cover you choose. Compare a few quotes, check the excess and limits, and make sure the provider is FCA authorised.
Can I insure business stock kept in a unit?
Usually through your business insurance. Tell your insurer the stock is kept at the unit and check any conditions on how it must be stored or locked.

pages.title: Storage Unit vs Garage or Spare Room | The Rock Factory
pages.desc: Is a storage unit worth it compared with your garage or spare room? A Blackpool guide to the real cost of space, using our prices only.
h1: or spare room: what is it really costing you?
pages.lead: Keeping things at home looks free. Sometimes it is. Sometimes it quietly costs you a room, a parking space or a working garage. This guide helps you weigh it up honestly.

sections.h2: Home storage is not always free
sections.html:
A garage full of boxes does not send you a bill. But it has a cost, just a hidden one. Your car sits on the drive or the street. The workbench is buried. The spare room cannot be a guest room, an office or a hobby space.

None of this means you should rent storage. For many people, keeping things at home is the right answer. The point is to compare like with like: what you would pay for a unit against what you give up by keeping things at home.

This guide uses only our own prices, because they are the only ones we can state with confidence.
